paragraphs: Iran has called the US response to its seven conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz "unconvincing", according to Al Jazeera, as President Donald Trump confirmed US strikes on an Iranian island near the waterway. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, wrote on X that Washington "must fully and explicitly address Iran's seven conditions and act upon them", and that only then would the strait be reopened.

The indirect talks center on an Iranian proposal to reopen the waterway over two days if the US meets Tehran's demands, which include lifting sanctions and ending a US naval blockade. Qatar's foreign ministry spokesperson, Majed al-Ansari, said talks were continuing, that both sides "remain committed to the negotiation process", and that Qatar was facilitating a real-time exchange of proposals.

Trump told Fox News the strikes hit an anti-aircraft facility, calling them a "minor attack" that "wasn't war". Iranian media said the strikes hit Qeshm Island. US officials told US media the strikes were defensive and followed Iranian fire at an American aircraft. Trump also repeated warnings of further action: "If we have to, we'll have to."

Al Jazeera, citing US media reports that relied on US officials, said Central Command had prepared plans for strikes that could begin as early as Wednesday, after the midterm elections, when three American aircraft carriers would be in the region. Iran's supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, ordered the military at the weekend to respond immediately to any threat and to update its target list.

Shipping was hit again. The UKMTO said two unidentified projectiles struck a tanker's engine room northeast of Oman's Limah, with no casualties reported. Separately, the Revolutionary Guard claimed four tankers struck mines and that it had seized two vessels, an account Al Jazeera said could not be independently verified.

North Korea fired several missiles toward the Sea of Japan on Wednesday, according to South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff, which said the launches were detected from the Sondok area on the country's eastern coast. Authorities in South Korea and the United States were analyzing the details. Al Jazeera reported it was Pyongyang's fourth such weapons launch in a month.

The launches came hours after North Korea denied involvement in the theft of more than $6 billion in crypto assets from Binance. Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, said on Friday that hackers had stolen the funds in what appears to be the largest crypto heist on record. The FBI later attributed the theft to North Korean hackers, naming a group known as TraderTraitor, which it said was also behind a $1.5 billion hack of the Bybit exchange last year.

North Korea dismissed the FBI announcement as "a trite provocation". Kim Yo Jong, the sister of leader Kim Jong Un, called it "an extension of Washington's invariable hostile policy" and ruled out dialogue until the US abandoned that policy. "We have no need to sit face to face with such unreliable and hostile persons," she said.

The statement follows President Donald Trump's remark in August that he plans to meet Kim later this year. Talks between the two ended abruptly in 2019 amid disagreements over North Korea's nuclear program. In October, the US, South Korea and Japan again called for the complete denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula.

Analysts told Al Jazeera that North Korea's accelerated weapons testing this year is likely a bid to increase its leverage in any future diplomacy. On Tuesday, state media said it had tested a new cluster warhead for strategic cruise missiles, and also reported that Kim visited a naval shipyard building a destroyer.

A public inquiry into the $368 billion Aukus nuclear submarine agreement has called it "the worst, riskiest and most costly defence decision ever made by an Australian government" and urged its immediate termination, The Guardian reported. The inquiry was led by former Labor MP and Midnight Oil frontman Peter Garrett and former defence chief Adm Chris Barrie. The Guardian described it as dominated by critics of the deal with the UK and US.

Its report, titled Surrendering Australia: the Aukus Deception, recommends suspending plans for new bases and holding a royal commission. It argues that hosting powerful nuclear submarines risks dragging Australia into conflict with China, undermines sovereignty and undercuts nonproliferation commitments. It also calls for a rework of the agreement's second pillar on technology sharing and for independent reviews by the auditor general and parliament.

Garrett said Labor had failed to conduct a thorough review since taking office. He said the Stirling precinct in Perth risked becoming a "de facto US base" hosting as many as 2,000 American personnel. Barrie said the plan was "not tenable". The inquiry estimates an additional $180 billion will be needed for nuclear waste. The government's preferred cost measure is 0.15% of GDP over the deal's lifetime.

The Guardian noted that Labor supports the deal, which was negotiated under the Morrison government, and that Donald Trump agreed to back it after a 2025 Pentagon review. Australia is due to begin receiving secondhand Virginia class submarines around 2032, though delays in US production have led to skepticism. Former prime ministers Paul Keating and Malcolm Turnbull are among prominent critics. The government's response to the report was not included in the article.

Hackers raised the temperatures of refrigeration systems at supermarkets in Germany, Romania and the United Kingdom during Monday's cyberattacks, officials said, bringing the number of affected European countries to at least 11, according to Al Jazeera. The European Union promised a collective response and said the attacks, which spoiled tonnes of food, were "not isolated". No one has claimed responsibility and the motive is unknown.

Problems were reported on Monday in nine EU countries: Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal and Sweden. Officials and companies said four supermarkets in Germany and six in Romania were hit on Tuesday. EU spokesperson Thomas Regnier said agencies were working with national authorities on a joint response but declined to name any culprits.

Dan Cimpean, head of Romania's National Cyber Security Directorate, told AFP the attack "seems semi-amateurish" and that officials did not suspect a state actor. Belgian federal prosecutors opened an investigation. In Italy, about 20 supermarkets were affected, and Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's office said the impact was "limited". In the UK, the National Cyber Security Centre's Richard Horne said hackers targeted small meat-processing firms with minimal impact.

The attacks mirrored an October cyberattack that swept hundreds of French supermarkets. Sweden's Coop said affected refrigerators at seven stores were connected to old 4G networks and that it was speeding an upgrade to 5G. Danish refrigeration maker Danfoss recommended that its systems not be directly accessible from the internet, and a Deloitte expert urged retailers to check whether their controllers were online and fully updated.

South Africans voted in local elections on Wednesday amid deep discontent over water outages, power cuts and crumbling infrastructure. The Guardian reported that the African National Congress is likely to remain the largest party but is polling below a third of the vote, down from 45.6% in the 2021 municipal elections and 40.2% in the 2024 national elections. A BBC-cited Ipsos poll put the party at 30%.

Much of the focus is on Gauteng province, where Johannesburg, Ekurhuleni and Tshwane are all run by coalitions. The Guardian said Johannesburg has had 10 mayors in 10 years and has faced water shortages for more than a week. The Democratic Alliance leads polls in all three metros but is not above 40%. The ANC's national leadership is reportedly open to working with it, while local ANC leaders are reportedly not in favor.

In Durban's eThekwini, the party of former president Jacob Zuma, uMkhonto we Sizwe, is polling above 40%, according to The Guardian. The Democratic Alliance looks set to keep Cape Town, probably with a smaller share than in 2021.

President Cyril Ramaphosa has denied his party is in decline, telling supporters at a Sunday rally, "the ANC is going higher and higher". Residents told the BBC of rubbish, water and electricity problems. Some said they would not vote because nothing changes, while first-time voter Sanele Ntombela hoped voting would bring change.
The electoral commission has a week to announce final results. Parties then have two weeks to form councils and elect mayors, since mayors are not directly elected.

Delhi's air quality has deteriorated as winter sets in, with the Air Quality Index standing at 377 on Wednesday morning, the BBC reported. India's pollution watchdog classifies readings from 301 to 400 as "very poor" and anything above 400 as "severe". Authorities have invoked Stage II of the Graded Response Action Plan, which introduces measures to curb dust, vehicle emissions and other pollution sources.

The rise follows an unusually clean October, when Delhi recorded its lowest average AQI for the month in eight years. Experts attributed the change to falling temperatures, slow winds and more crop-residue burning in Punjab and Haryana. A recent storm had cleared the air, but north-westerly winds returned and carried smoke from burning fields toward the capital.

Diwali is days away, and fireworks often worsen the city's pollution. Last year, Delhi woke to a toxic haze the morning after the festival despite a court directive to use less-polluting firecrackers. On Monday, India's Supreme Court allowed the manufacture, sale and use of certified green firecrackers in Delhi and nearby areas for a limited period. They may be set off only between 6 and 7 a.m. and between 8 and 10 p.m. on November 7 and 8, and not within 300 meters of hospitals, care homes, schools and other silence zones.

The court acknowledged that conventional firecrackers had continued to be sold as green ones, even during a complete ban. It directed police to patrol sales areas, make random QR-code checks and seize illegal products. Mumbai, which hit an AQI of 322 on October 24, recorded a "satisfactory" 89 on Wednesday.

An Ethiopian-born American citizen and former US contractor has pleaded guilty to passing highly classified intelligence to Ethiopia, the BBC reported. The US Department of Justice said Abraham Teklu Lemma, 54, admitted sharing dozens of classified documents and photographs with senior Ethiopian officials over more than two years. He pleaded guilty to conspiring to transmit national defense information to a foreign government.

Prosecutors said Lemma worked as a contractor at the State Department, Justice Department and National Reconnaissance Office. They said he removed classified material from secure facilities, sometimes in handwritten notes, and used his role as an IT administrator to extract electronic files. Much of the material concerned Ethiopia's armed conflict and included satellite imagery and details of military activities, sent by encrypted messages.

The FBI said Ethiopian officials used the intelligence in military operations. Prosecutors said Lemma hoped it would help Ethiopia's military identify and kill paramilitary fighters. Court papers cited a December 2021 message in which he wrote, "We have to finish these people once and for all, otherwise there will never be peace in Ethiopia," and later urged the official to send drones.

US Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro said he "betrayed his oath, his colleagues, and his country". He was arrested in Maryland in August 2023. He faces up to 22 years in prison under a plea agreement, with sentencing set for April 14, 2027.

The conflict began in November 2020, pitting federal forces and allies against Tigray fighters, and the BBC said it killed hundreds of thousands of people. A peace agreement in November 2022 ended the main fighting, though insecurity has persisted.

Google defended a new policy on artificial intelligence in schools on Tuesday after criticism from elected officials, CNBC reported. In a blog post, Google said it is bringing AI into its Classroom offering with a product called Guided Learning. The New York Times reported that the company will turn off Search for schools that reject AI entirely.

Sen. Bernie Sanders and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani criticized the reported policy on social media. Mamdani wrote that Google was "trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools", and Sanders called the policy "extortion". Former FTC Chair Lina Khan said it showed the danger of letting an unregulated monopolist control an essential service.

Google responded on X that the policy was meant to give schools more choice. It said Gemini, Gemini Notebook and Search are turned off by default and that "schools are in control" of turning them on. It added that AI Mode and AI Overviews in Search for schools will offer step-by-step guided learning so students do not get quick answers to schoolwork.

CNBC noted that Google's post did not directly address the claim that Search access requires accepting AI. Chris Phillips, Google's vice president for education, told the Times that "Search and AI are deeply integrated." Google referred CNBC to its X post.

The episode follows other scrutiny. Common Sense Media recently gave Google's AI Overviews an "unacceptable risk" rating, and last month Sens. Richard Blumenthal and Josh Hawley opened an inquiry into Google's push of AI into classrooms. Google has also lost antitrust cases over its search and advertising businesses.

Anthropic is working on an open source system to verify which AI model produced a given output, according to a blog post published Tuesday and reported by TechCrunch. The system, called FlashProve, is built to provide what researchers call "provable inference": a cryptographic proof that an output came from a specific model. It is meant to let users confirm that an answer came from the model they think they are using.

The researchers compare it to cryptographic email signatures. They say it would resist impostors disguising one model as another, even when the impostor is the lab that runs the model. They say it could stop a company from secretly swapping in a cheaper model to cut costs, or a more expensive one to inflate performance results. It could also check third-party claims, such as that software was scanned by a frontier cybersecurity model.

To work, the system requires AI labs to publish a "fingerprint" of each model they release, which can later be matched to specific outputs and verified cryptographically. The fingerprints do not reveal a model's weights, the internal numbers that closed-model makers such as Anthropic and OpenAI keep private. That means commercial models could be covered without labs giving up that asset. The system is also designed to be lightweight enough for verification on a local device.

Researchers released a technical specification and working code under an open source license on GitHub. The work is ongoing, and there are no plans to deploy it at Anthropic or any other lab. The researchers said the post shares "intermediate progress, and not a completed research agenda", and that they hope others will improve on it.

Some AI data centers stuck in long waits for grid connections and new turbines are generating their own electricity with converted jet engines, according to a New York Times report summarized by TechCrunch. The engines are pulled from retired aircraft and rebuilt to burn natural gas.

The main appeal is speed. Rystad Energy analyst Audun Martinsen told the Times that with jet-powered units, "they can have a data center running in 24 months." By comparison, the International Energy Agency says connecting 100 megawatts to the grid in Northern Virginia takes about seven years. A Mitsubishi Power executive told Bloomberg last week that most power capacity is expected to come on by 2031.

The delays are already costing some operators business. Last month Microsoft pulled out as anchor customer for Nscale's data center in Loughton, England, after the local utility said it could not deliver enough power until the early to mid-2030s.

Elon Musk's xAI is among the users, having installed eight converted turbines in Mississippi to help power its Colossus 2 data center in Memphis, the Times reported, citing state permits and satellite imagery. They come from ProEnergy, which rebuilds a GE engine commonly found on Boeing jets. Crusoe, which is building OpenAI's first Stargate site in Abilene, Texas, ordered 13 ProEnergy units in April.

There are trade-offs. According to the Times, converted jet engines are less efficient and pollute more than turbines designed for conventional gas plants, and more of them are needed to make the same amount of power. Some experts say efficiency and environmental concerns may grow in importance in a year or two, which could make the engines a short-term play. The Trump administration, the report adds, is encouraging data centers to generate their own electricity.

European missile maker MBDA is aiming for its planned high-speed strike missile, Stratus RS, to have a range "far, far, far" greater than the Exocet anti-ship missile, which reaches more than 200 kilometers, said Olivier Gauffin, the company's deputy director for sales and business development. He spoke at a briefing at the Euronaval exhibition in Paris on Tuesday, according to Defense News.

Stratus RS, for rapid strike, is being developed for France and the United Kingdom. MBDA is awaiting a development contract from France's Directorate General for Armament on behalf of both partners. Gauffin said the high supersonic missile would cover four missions, including deep strike and anti-ship strike, and suppression and destruction of enemy air defenses. It would also target large aircraft such as airborne warning systems and tankers. He said it will use a throttleable liquid ramjet engine and be highly maneuverable.

MBDA is also working on a stealthy subsonic cruise missile, Stratus LO, for France, the U.K. and Italy. Gauffin described the pair as one "more a Ferrari" and the other "a stealth truck." Defense News noted that NATO has called on European allies to rebuild offensive capabilities, and that Stratus RS would fill a gap, since European militaries mostly lack weapons able to destroy air defenses.

Both missiles are planned to be air-launched from aircraft including the Rafale and Eurofighter Typhoon. Ships or land launchers would use a booster. MBDA expects flight testing to start before the end of the decade and service entry at the beginning of the 2030s. Gauffin said full development should start "very soon."

Because of its size, Stratus RS would not fit NATO-standard torpedo tubes and is not envisaged for submarines, Gauffin said. MBDA also presented an updated Naval Cruise Missile, with production to start in early 2030 and a range of more than 1,000 km, and is likewise waiting for a DGA development contract.

Sierra Nevada Corporation is no longer competing for the Navy's new training jet, Breaking Defense reported, leaving Textron Aviation Defense and its M-346N as the only known major competitor. SNC said in a statement that it "could not responsibly bid" the Undergraduate Jet Training System program "under the current contract structure," while remaining "committed to naval jet training" and ready to re-engage if the approach is revisited.

Textron confirmed it submitted the M-346N to the Navy by the Oct. 30 proposal deadline, which the program office said was held after an earlier extension from June 30. A Textron spokesperson said the firm is "ready to support the U.S. Navy and its future training needs." Breaking Defense wrote that, barring a reopened competition or a surprise entrant, the M-346N appears to be the de facto winner. It noted that Stavatti Aerospace said on Oct. 30 it had also submitted a bid.

The field had already thinned. Lockheed Martin said in April it would not offer the TF-50N with Korea Aerospace Industries, and Boeing said in June it would drop out. In September, Breaking Defense reported that Northrop Grumman was leaving SNC's bid, which was built around a clean-sheet design called the Freedom.

The Navy now estimates it will award a contract between July and the end of September 2027, later than the June 2027 target in a September request for proposals and the original March 2027 plan. The program is meant to replace the T-45 Goshawk, which entered service in the early 1990s. The Navy said in March that the new jet need not land on carriers or support field carrier landing practice to touch down, though it must support wave-offs.

California is accepting $1.42 billion in federal broadband grant money while rejecting a condition that it stop enforcing its net neutrality law and other telecom rules, Ars Technica reported. The California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) set out its position in a letter to Arielle Roth, who leads the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA).

The money comes from the $42 billion BEAD program. According to Ars, the NTIA decided last year that states must agree not to enforce rate regulation or net neutrality rules on internet providers that receive BEAD funds. California is slated to spend $1.42 billion to connect 270,571 locations and may ultimately receive up to $1.86 billion.

CPUC President John Reynolds wrote that the commission "cannot be bound by any terms or conditions that are unconstitutional or not authorized by law" and does not waive any challenge to the condition. He said the CPUC cannot stop other California agencies from enforcing state law, and called the federal condition "vague and ambiguous." The state will not distribute funds to providers until differences with the NTIA are resolved, and California could sue if the NTIA does not change its position.

The NTIA appears unlikely to bend. A spokesperson told Ars that the award's terms are the entire agreement and that the CPUC's letter is not part of it. The consumer group Public Knowledge backed California, calling the demand "brazen and meritless" and saying the NTIA lacks authority to alter state law. Ars reported that providers receiving BEAD funding could be exempt from such state laws for up to 14 years.
Possible next steps include legal challenges involving the state, the federal government and providers seeking funds.

Indonesia on Sunday formally asked Russia to stop recruiting Indonesian citizens to fight in Ukraine, Foreign Policy reported in its Southeast Asia Brief. The request followed word from Ukraine's Defense Intelligence that Taufiq Muhammad, a Jakarta taxi driver in his 40s, died in battle in May after about a week and a half of training under a Russian military contract.

His death was the latest in a series of cases. A former Indonesian Marine and a former Brimob police officer were confirmed to have joined Russian forces and lost their citizenship, and a 30-year-old Indonesian man was reportedly killed in a drone strike in September. Indonesian police said on Monday that cases involving 58 citizens are under investigation. Indonesia's ambassador in Russia said in September he had taken dozens of calls from families fearing relatives had been recruited.

Indonesia is not alone. Ukrainian data published by StopRussianRecruiters.org lists 44 Southeast Asian prisoners of war, including 16 Vietnamese, 14 Filipinos and 10 Indonesians. Analyst Munira Mustaffa compared Russia's social media recruitment to scam-center tactics, saying many men were lured by promises of blue-collar work. She said Southeast Asians are a small fraction of recruits compared with South Asia, Central Asia and Africa, though a Tagesschau investigation in July found Russia targeting Cambodia, Indonesia and Malaysia.

Indonesian academic Radityo Dharmaputra called the government's step "necessary, albeit ineffective." He urged President Prabowo Subianto to appeal personally to Vladimir Putin, and suggested public pressure and an ASEAN framework. Foreign Policy described the regional response as muted; the Philippines announced an investigation into illegal recruitment in October. Russia's response was not reported in the piece.

Canada has joined a growing group of countries refusing to play ice hockey against Russia. Prime Minister Mark Carney said Tuesday that Russian skaters will not be able to compete in a world junior championship next month because of the war in Ukraine, The Guardian reported.

"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified, horrific war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," Carney told reporters. The tournament is scheduled to begin on 26 December in Alberta.

The dispute follows a decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) to allow Russians to compete in International Ice Hockey Federation events. The federation's ban took effect after Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022 and had been extended annually. After several appeals by Russia's hockey federation, CAS lifted the ban on Friday, saying safety and security worries "were not supported by sufficient evidence."

On Monday the Finnish Ice Hockey Association asked other nations to stand against the ruling. Federations in Denmark, Sweden, Norway, Latvia and the Czech Republic said Tuesday they sided with Finland. Norway's federation said its position that Russia should be excluded remains unchanged and that playing Russia could expose its players and staff to significant security risks.

Ukraine's foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, thanked European nations and urged others to refuse to play Russia and deny visas to its players. The CAS ruling has also left cities worldwide to decide whether to host upcoming tournaments as planned if Russians compete. The Guardian did not include a response from Russia's federation.

Prince William has said the prospect of more wildfires in the UK because of climate change is "terrifying" and that preparation will be "crucial," the BBC reported. He spoke during a visit to Treherbert in Rhondda Cynon Taf, which was threatened by a large mountain fire in August, and praised a "gargantuan" effort to protect homes, land and lives.

"We need to start taking wildfires as seriously as the continent has done," he said, raising issues including a lack of firefighting aircraft. He told firefighters that 2026 was the first summer he had felt "generally worried about the scale of the wildfires in the country."

South Wales Fire and Rescue Service declared a major incident in August when it had to respond to 14 wildfires at once. Crews came from 22 other UK fire services, and soldiers, including 200 Gurkha logistics troops, dug fire breaks and helped supply 2.1 million litres of water. Aled Bound, a firefighter, called it the hardest wildfire season he had dealt with and warned it "could well be a sign of what's to come." Figures from the National Fire Chiefs Council show a record 1,350 significant wildfires across England and Wales, up more than 300 on 2025.

The BBC said the government recently announced that RAF Chinook helicopters and A400M aircraft would be equipped to fight fires, and a Welsh government wildfire summit promised action on preparedness. Deputy chief fire officer Adam Openshaw said lessons had been learned and measures would follow the summits.
Locals also kept the community centre open around the clock for days, and it became a control hub. Kath Edwards of the charity Valleys Kids said the community pulled together.

Kellogg's has stopped using rice grains in Rice Krispies and Coco Pops in the UK, citing "changing weather conditions" that have disrupted supplies, the BBC reported. A company spokesperson said on Tuesday that corn flour and rice flour are being used instead.

The BBC said dry weather in key producing countries in Asia has hit crops, reducing harvests and pushing up prices. The new recipes mean packaging will now carry a "contains wheat gluten" warning. Kellogg's said the changes will help "maintain consistent quality" while weather affects the quality and availability of some rice and grains. It said the updated recipes were "carefully assessed," that customer feedback was considered, and that it appreciates even small changes to a loved product "can feel noticeable."

The company said the cereals still meet UK food standards on fat, salt and sugar, contain no artificial colours, flavours or sweeteners, and keep the same nutritional benefits such as fibre, vitamin D and iron.

The change applies only in the UK. A spokesperson for Kellogg's North American business told the BBC that Rice Krispies in the US and Canada will continue to be made with real rice, with no recipe changes expected. The BBC noted that the Kellogg company split into two firms in 2023: Kellanova, now owned by Mars, which sells cereals and snacks globally, and WK Kellogg's, which operates in North America and has been taken over by Ferrero.

The BBC reported that droughts, floods and heatwaves linked to El Niño have affected much of Asia, which grows most of the world's rice. The World Meteorological Agency expects the record-breaking El Niño to last until at least 2027.

Nexus Mods, a major PC gaming mod repository, is making AI disclosure mandatory for new uploads. Authors will have to declare "whether AI has been used in their work," the site announced as part of a broader post on AI-generated content, according to The Verge.

Site owner Victor "Foledinho" Folmann wrote that a consistent concern from users is that it is not clearly disclosed when AI has been used to create a mod. The site already has tags for AI-generated and AI-assisted mods, and these will become more prominent on mod pages. Mods tagged AI-assisted must also include a public explanation of how and where AI was used.

Folmann said Nexus Mods is "pro-human creativity" but will not introduce an outright ban on AI-generated mods. His reasoning was that AI is used throughout creation, from script autocompletion to textures, voices and full assets, so a clear boundary is hard to draw. A ban, he argued, would not eliminate AI but would stop people mentioning it. He said the site would prefer AI use be out in the open and clearly labelled.

Folmann also said the site will not use mods to train AI and will not sell or license them to anyone who does. It is working on clearer controls over how mods can be reused by others and on stronger attribution when one mod uses another author's mod with permission.

Other changes include limits on how many mods from one author appear at a time in the Recently Added section, tighter restrictions on uploads from new accounts, and controls to hide AI-generated content on game pages and the homepage, with search next. Authors have 60 days, until January 2nd, to update existing mods before enforcement begins.

Democrats have won control of both chambers of Congress, according to an NPR analysis based on Associated Press race calls. The Washington Examiner reported that the party reached the 218 House seats needed early Wednesday, citing the AP, when Johnny Garcia won Texas's 35th District, a seat redrawn in 2025 to favor Republicans.

In the Senate, NPR said seven seats flipped from Republican control: North Carolina, South Carolina, Ohio, Texas, Kansas, Iowa and Maine. Republicans began the year with a 53-47 majority. Fox News reported that Democrats had clinched five pickups at one point, with Michigan, Minnesota and Alaska still undecided. The Washington Examiner reported at least 54 Democratic seats. The differing counts appear to reflect timing.

House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is poised to become speaker, said voters had "had enough of the extremism, enough of the corruption." Speaker Mike Johnson said Republicans had known they would have to "defy more than a century of midterm history." Senate Majority Leader John Thune said Republicans would not stand idly by as what he called the "far-left, socialist wing" of the Democratic Party tries to unwind their work.

Divided government is expected to bring conflict. Trump told a podcast he would become "Mr. Veto" but that "at some point we'll probably make deals." NPR noted that Democrats must work with Republicans on must-pass bills such as the 12 annual appropriations bills. Senate control will also halt the steady confirmation of Trump's judges.

Democrats have signaled investigations. Rep. Robert Garcia, expected to chair the House Oversight Committee, posted "LAWYER UP." Asked about impeachment, Jeffries said Democrats "haven't ruled anything in, and we haven't ruled anything out," according to the Washington Examiner. The Examiner also reported that Jeffries's path to the speakership could be complicated by progressive freshmen seeking concessions. Fox News reported that several incoming senators have been noncommittal about backing Chuck Schumer as leader.

Democrat James Talarico has won the U.S. Senate race in Texas, defeating Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton, according to The Guardian and Fox News. The Fox News Decision Desk called the race shortly after 11 p.m. Eastern on Tuesday. The Guardian said no Democrat had won a Senate seat in Texas since Lloyd Bentsen in 1988, or any statewide office since 1994. Trump carried the state by nearly 14 points in 2024.

Talarico, 37, a state representative, former middle school teacher and Presbyterian seminarian, told supporters in Austin: "We just took back Texas!" He compared the race to David and Goliath and named Elon Musk and Trump as his opponents. He will replace John Cornyn, who lost a Republican primary to Paxton after Trump backed Paxton.

The race was among the most expensive Senate contests ever, with advertising topping $500 million, according to estimates cited by The Guardian. It said Republican-aligned groups spent heavily for Paxton, including money linked to Musk, whom Talarico accused of trying to buy a seat. Talarico's campaign said it raised $64 million in the third quarter.

The candidates drew sharp contrasts. Talarico highlighted Paxton's 2023 impeachment by the Texas House, after which the state senate acquitted him, and securities fraud charges resolved in 2024 under an agreement; Paxton denied wrongdoing. Paxton called Talarico "the most radical Democrat ever to run statewide" and a democratic socialist, a label Talarico's campaign rejected, according to Fox News. Fox said he styled himself a moderate. Trump called him "Talafreako." The Guardian said some Republican claims about him were false or challenged by factcheckers.
Cornyn congratulated Talarico on X and offered help with his transition. Fox News also reported that its desk projected Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeating Gov. Greg Abbott.

President Trump said on election night that he is willing to accept the midterm results, while arguing his party would have won big had he been a candidate. "I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!" he wrote on social media, according to The Guardian. The paper noted he had spent months urging supporters to pretend he was on the ballot.

Trump told the New York Times he is "absolutely willing to accept those results" and ready to work with Democrats. "We'll probably work something out," he said. He also pointed to his veto power. "They'll send over things that are insane and I'll veto them," he told Fox News, predicting that after a couple of months Democrats would ask how to get things done and "we'll work together."

The Guardian reported that the results included Democratic Senate wins in Kansas, Texas and South Carolina, plus Roy Cooper's defeat of Michael Whatley in North Carolina and Jon Ossoff's re-election in Georgia. It said the vote was widely seen as a referendum on Trump's leadership. Concerns about the cost of living, rising fuel prices and an unpopular war with Iran loomed over the campaign, and Trump's approval rating was at record lows, according to the paper.

The Guardian also said Trump held 30 rallies in the past month. It reported that he told voters the US would stop $4 billion in annual funding to Israel after the end of this year. It described his campaign message, which cast Democratic candidates as radical, as at odds with voter priorities, citing polls that show voters care more about their economic situation. Trump said Democrats had nominated what he called "the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history." The Guardian noted that the party out of power traditionally gains in midterms.

Democrat Troy Jackson has defeated Republican Sen. Susan Collins in Maine, according to race calls by the Associated Press and the Fox News Decision Desk. Collins called Jackson to concede on Tuesday night. The win ends her nearly three-decade Senate career and makes Jackson the first Democrat to represent Maine in the Senate since 1995, NPR reported.

Collins said in a statement it had been "the honor of my life" to serve, and said her staff would work for a smooth transition. Jackson wrote on X: "Maine, I owe you everything." A fifth-generation logger and former president of the Maine Senate, he ran on a progressive populist platform with ties to organized labor.

Jackson became the nominee after Graham Platner, the Democrats' original candidate, left the race following an allegation of rape, which Platner denies. NPR said Jackson replaced him in August, while Fox News and the Washington Examiner placed the change in July. The Examiner said Platner's nomination had also been marked by scandals over a tattoo and old social media posts. Fox News reported that Jackson's campaign was nearly derailed early when it emerged that his partner is also his second cousin.

The candidates argued over independence. Collins pitched herself as a needed centrist voice and cited her role as chair of the Appropriations Committee. Jackson argued the Iran war, tariffs and health care costs were hurting Maine more than her work helped. Democrats also cited her 2018 vote to confirm Brett Kavanaugh. Collins said she does not regret it and supports abortion protections. The Examiner noted she voted against last year's tax law and eventually opposed the war.
NPR said groups spent more than a quarter of a billion dollars on ads, according to AdImpact, and polls showed a virtual tie before voting ended.

Democrats flipped Senate seats in Kansas and South Carolina among other states, according to NPR and Fox News. In Kansas, pastor Adam Hamilton won, the first Democrat the state has sent to the Senate since 1932, NPR reported. The Fox News Decision Desk projected that pediatrician Annie Andrews defeated Republican Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina, making her the first Democrat in nearly three decades to win a Senate election there.

Hamilton, who leads the largest United Methodist church in the country, ran as an "independent-minded Democrat" after considering an independent bid. He called for term limits and criticized national Democrats. NPR said he took $5 million from a PAC associated with Chuck Schumer but said he would not back Schumer for another leadership post. Sen. Roger Marshall's campaign tried to tie Hamilton to Schumer 15 times in the final debate. NPR said the race was the most expensive in Kansas history.

The campaign turned personal. NPR said The New York Times reported that Marshall, a former OB-GYN, sued 700 former patients for medical debt, and Hamilton's campaign used one of them in an ad. Marshall's campaign ran an ad claiming Hamilton protected a pedophile, tied to abuse reports at a church camp. NPR said court records showed the church's first investigation was inconclusive, and Hamilton said he was not involved in the decision to let the volunteer return.

In South Carolina, Graham was appointed after her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, died in July, and then won a runoff primary. Fox News said Trump visited twice late in the race. Both Graham and Andrews focused on affordability. Democratic strategist Mally Smith said voters had rejected Trump's choice. Graham's campaign response was not included in the page text.

Democrats won several major governor's races on Tuesday, while Republicans held Florida. In Ohio, Democrat Amy Acton defeated Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, becoming the first Democrat and first woman to win the governorship in two decades, according to the BBC. She succeeds term-limited Gov. Mike DeWine. In California, Xavier Becerra, a former health secretary, beat Trump-endorsed Republican Steve Hilton and will be the state's first Latino governor since 1875, The Guardian reported.

The Ohio race turned bitter after Ramaswamy's campaign aired an ad featuring Acton's estranged mother, who said her daughter "lied her entire life." The BBC said the ad did not mention that her husband was charged with raping Acton as a child. Nikki Haley criticized it and DeWine called it "deeply troubling." Trump called it "powerful" and Vice President JD Vance said he was "a little bit disgusted" by Republican criticism. In his concession, Ramaswamy said he was rooting for Ohio and Acton. The BBC also reported that Sherrod Brown defeated Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio.

In Florida, Fox News projected that Rep. Byron Donalds, endorsed by Trump, beat Democrat David Jolly. It described him as the first Black person elected governor of Florida and the first Black Republican elected governor nationwide. He succeeds term-limited Ron DeSantis. Donalds said he would make life more affordable and keep streets safe. Fox said he accused Jolly of embracing "radical socialism"; Jolly called that a lie and said he has condemned the Democratic Socialists of America many times.

Becerra, 68, promised to defend California against Trump's agenda and cited suing the administration 122 times as state attorney general. The Guardian said he faces high costs, housing shortages and wildfire risk. The page text supplied does not cover the Georgia, Michigan or Wisconsin results.

Missouri voters defeated a ballot proposal that would have reimposed an abortion ban, according to an Associated Press race call reported by NPR. The result reaffirms the 2024 vote that lifted one of the country's strictest abortion bans. The proposal, Amendment 3, was placed on the ballot by the Republican-led legislature. It would have banned abortion for the first 12 weeks, with exceptions for rape and incest, and longer for fetal anomalies.

Its defeat keeps current law, which allows abortion until fetal viability, though some restrictions apply on how procedures are performed. NPR said Missouri was one of four states with abortion on the ballot this year. Since the Supreme Court struck down federal abortion protections in 2022, abortion law has become a patchwork from state to state.

The measure also joined the abortion ban in a single question with a ban on puberty blockers, hormone therapy and gender-affirming surgery for minors. NPR said Republican leaders, including Gov. Mike Kehoe, raised money and campaigned for it, but many supporting ads did not mention abortion and focused on the gender-affirming care ban. Opponents of abortion rights defended the approach. State Auditor Scott Fitzpatrick, a Republican, said abortion was "much closer to a 50/50 issue" while trans medical procedures were "probably more like an 80/20 issue."

Abortion rights supporters called the focus on gender-affirming care misdirection. They noted that care for minors is already banned by statute in Missouri, though the bans on puberty blockers and hormone therapy expire in 2027. NPR said the campaign against the measure raised more than $26 million in large donations this year, compared with about $6.7 million for the campaign backing it. The supplied page text does not cover the congressional map vote, Proposition A.

Democrats moved quickly after their midterm wins to warn the Trump administration of coming oversight, according to Fox News. Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, posted "LAWYER UP" on X. Sen. Ron Wyden of Oregon posted one word: "Subpoenas." Sen. Ed Markey of Connecticut wrote that new forests would be needed for all the subpoenas Democrats would print.

Garcia, in line to chair Oversight, has said the panel would examine the Trump family's business dealings, immigration enforcement, alleged corporate corruption and the handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files. He told Punchbowl News his team was "not starting from scratch." Fox reported that House rules let committees delegate subpoena authority to chairs, so some Democratic chairs could issue demands without Republican support. It noted that ignoring a subpoena can lead to contempt proceedings, but that forcing executive branch officials to comply, especially when they invoke privilege, can mean long legal battles.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, whom Fox calls War Secretary, could face particular scrutiny. Democrats have introduced articles of impeachment accusing him of offenses including waging an unauthorized war against Iran. Fox said Rep. Thomas Massie, a Republican, plans to force a vote on his own impeachment resolution in the lame-duck session.

House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, poised to be speaker, told supporters voters had sent a message against extremism and corruption. "We're going to bring accountability to those who have visited unprecedented corruption on this country," he said, according to NPR, adding that Democrats would focus on affordability. NPR noted that Trump retains his veto. Speaker Mike Johnson said Republicans faced a century of midterm history. The supplied page text does not include Republican responses to the investigation plans or to Jeffries's corruption framing.

Claire Valdez, a Democratic Socialists of America-backed candidate endorsed by New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, was projected to win New York's 7th Congressional District on Tuesday, according to Fox News. She defeated Republican Melvin Rivera in the race to succeed Rep. Nydia Velázquez, who is retiring after holding the seat since 1993. Fox said the district's strong Democratic lean made Valdez the favorite.

The contest was closely watched because of the June primary, when Valdez beat a field that included Brooklyn Borough President Antonio Reynoso, who had backing from more established Democrats, including Velázquez. Fox reported that Valdez ran on abolishing ICE, a Green New Deal-style climate approach, universal rent control and Medicare for All. DSA said she was the only candidate in the race committed to refusing money from the real estate industry.

Fox also said Darializa Avila Chevalier, another DSA candidate, beat Rep. Adriano Espaillat, chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, in a primary. The page text supplied does not describe the general election results for her or for Brad Lander.

Fox presented the wins as a point of tension within the party. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries did not endorse in the 7th District race but said in June that Velázquez, Attorney General Letitia James, the Working Families Party and many unions were on one side, with DSA on the other. Democratic strategist Mally Smith told Fox that Valdez's win was unsurprising given how blue the district is, and said that to win competitive states the party should nominate candidates like Roy Cooper and James Talarico. Sen. John Fetterman criticized some slogans from the left, saying some colleagues refuse to call them out. Mamdani's response was not included in the supplied page text.

An election day poll of more than 79,000 voters found the economy and the state of democracy to be the top issues, according to the BBC. The survey, called the Voter Poll, is conducted by SSRS for a consortium of news organizations and includes early and election day voters. The BBC cautioned that the figures are estimates that could change as more data arrives.

Thirty-nine percent named the economy as the most important issue and 32 percent named the state of democracy. Immigration followed at 14 percent. Seventy-five percent rated the national economy as not so good or poor, and 44 percent said their family finances were worse than two years ago. Sixty-five percent said Trump's policies had worsened economic conditions, while 27 percent said they had improved them.

On Trump as a factor, 43 percent said expressing opposition to him was a reason for their vote, 41 percent said he was not a factor, and 16 percent said expressing support was a reason. Seventy-nine percent said inflation had caused their family severe or moderate hardship, and 62 percent said higher prices were more because of Trump's policies. Sixty-three percent said the US made the wrong decision in taking military action against Iran, and 74 percent said the conflict was a crucial or major factor in their congressional vote. Ninety percent said government corruption was a crucial or major factor.

The poll also gave breakdowns of House votes. Women backed Democrats 58 percent to 40 percent, while men were nearly evenly split. Voters under 45 favored Democrats by almost two to one. Voters 45 to 64 backed them 51 percent to 48 percent, and those over 65 leaned slightly Republican. White voters favored Republicans 51 percent to 48 percent, and Hispanic and Latino voters favored Democrats 62 percent to 35 percent. Voters without a college degree favored Republicans 51 percent to 47 percent, while college graduates favored Democrats 62 percent to 36 percent.
